name: The Control Chamber
description: Software-Defined Networking, Automation, and Programmability. The modern networker's arsenal.

nodes.name: The Bifurcation Gate
nodes.description: Understanding the separation of Control Plane and Data Plane

encounters.scenario: The network's central nervous system is splitting! A logic virus is trying to confuse the switches by mixing 'decision-making' instructions with 'packet-moving' instructions. You must sort the incoming streams to stabilize the architecture.
encounters.question:
Sort the following functions into their correct plane:
1. Calculating the Spanning Tree topology
2. Forwarding a frame from Port 1 to Port 5
3. Building the Routing Table via OSPF
4. Inspecting a packet header to determine destination MAC
encounters.explanation: Control Plane: 1 & 3 (Spanning Tree calc, Routing Table building). Data Plane: 2 & 4 (Frame forwarding, MAC inspection). The Control Plane is the 'brain' that decides where traffic goes. The Data Plane is the 'muscle' that moves the bits.
encounters.practical_emulation: Drag-and-drop: Sort functional blocks into Control Plane vs Data Plane containers

nodes.name: The Orchestrator's Console
nodes.description: Centralized network management via SDN Controllers

encounters.scenario: A massive VLAN reconfiguration is required across 40 access switches simultaneously. Manual CLI entry will take hours and lead to human error. You are logged into the SDN Controller.
encounters.question: What is the most efficient SDN-based method to apply this change across the entire fabric?
options: SSH into each switch individually and configure the VLAN
Push a centralized policy from the SDN Controller
Send a broadcast packet to all switches
Physically visit each switch with a console cable
encounters.explanation: The SDN Controller uses Southbound APIs (OpenFlow, NETCONF) to push configurations to all managed devices from a single point, ensuring consistency and speed.
encounters.practical_emulation: Dashboard selection: Choose 'Centralized Policy Push' vs 'Individual Device CLI'

nodes.name: The Syntax Void
nodes.description: Debugging automation scripts and JSON configurations

encounters.scenario: The automation script is failing! The SDN Controller returns '400 Bad Request'. You've intercepted the JSON payload but it looks corrupted.
encounters.objective: Identify the syntax error in the JSON configuration
encounters.hint: Look at the line before 'mtu'. Does it end properly?
encounters.explanation: Missing comma after 'true'. In JSON, key-value pairs must be separated by commas except the last one.
encounters.practical_emulation: Code editor: Click the exact line/character where the syntax error exists

nodes.name: The API Gateway
nodes.description: REST API methods and endpoint construction

encounters.scenario: You need to build a monitoring dashboard. Your script must ask the network controller for the current status of interface 'TenGigabitEthernet0/1'.
encounters.question: Which HTTP method should your script use to RETRIEVE this information?
encounters.explanation: GET is used to retrieve data from a server. POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes.
encounters.practical_emulation: cURL builder: Select correct verb and type endpoint path

nodes.name: The Architect's Forge
nodes.description: Choosing the right automation tool for the job

encounters.scenario: The CTO has given you three automation mandates. Choose the correct tool for each mission.
encounters.question:
Mission A: Quick one-time config change to 5 switches without installing software.
Mission B: Maintain 'Desired State' on 500 switches with drift detection.
Mission C: Custom logic script to integrate with proprietary database.
options: A: Ansible, B: Puppet/Chef, C: Python
A: Puppet, B: Ansible, C: Bash
A: Python, B: Ansible, C: Puppet
A: Chef, B: Python, C: Ansible
encounters.explanation: A: Ansible (agentless, push-based, good for one-offs). B: Puppet/Chef (agent-based, continuous state compliance). C: Python (ultimate flexibility for custom logic).
encounters.practical_emulation: Drag tool icons onto mission briefing cards
